In fact, a sufficiently well-heeled community could, today, buy a commercial floating nuclear reactor from a couple of nations. Russia has long been in development of these as a potential export product, seeing them as a safer and more convenient way to deploy nuclear energy in remote areas and developing countries. But they require refueling every few years and are based on outdated nuclear fuel ecologies. Lithium based systems would be more practical as the fuel would be more freely sourced from around the world, but this remains undeveloped with the most work on it being done by the Chinese.

The far more practical choice of energy for a marine settlement is OTEC as this provides an 'engine' for, energy, fresh water, food production, and fuels for transportation while producing some exportable industrial product and carbon credits through offset and sequester. There is no political/environmental controversy involved in deploying the technology, no dependency on mainland nations for fuel, and commercial developers currently exist. It's chief limitation is limited scalability. Just like a nuclear power plant, it's in the half-to-a-billion dollar range. You can't really start small with it. But then the average cruise liner is a half billion dollar proposition too.

Also, there aren't really any abandoned oil rigs at sea you can simply 'take over'. None exist outside the economic territories of nations. You see, the territorial limits aren't the 20 miles out people typically assume. Thanks to strong-arming by the Reagan administration in the '80s, an Exclusive Economic Zone provision was added to the international Law of the Sea that extends the territories of nations with an economic development zone 200 miles out to sea. And this specifically targets such things as creating artificial islands and stationary floating structures. (because Reagan was in a trade war with Japan at the time and wanted to obstruct Japanese industrialists' plans to create a floating airport off the coast of Hawaii intended to accommodate a Hawaiian retirement living craze among the Japanese upper-class. 200 miles is the range limit of typical commercial helicopters. This came back to haunt us later when Bush I wanted to establish oil-rig based interdiction facilities in the Persian Gulf and suddenly discovered that, thanks to his own previous finagling, international waters weren't international anymore...) So now, if you want political autonomy and the freedom to do industrial/commercial activity at sea, you have to be able to operate very far out or use always moving boats flying some flag of convenience.
